record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in the Dynamics of Quadratic and Higher Degree Polynomial ODE Systems
record.context_brief: classification and counting of chaotic polynomial systems
record.original_question: For autonomous polynomial systems x_i' = P_i(x) of degree at most k in N variables, determine which systems can have chaotic solutions after quotienting by natural equivalences. In particular: for N = 3 and given k, after eliminating scalar rescalings of the variables and time and quotienting by the order-three permutation group, determine which systems are chaotic, how many chaotic systems exist, and among them how many are conservative or dissipative; for N > 3 and given k, answer the analogous counting and classification question after quotienting by coordinate rescalings and the full permutation group; more generally, answer the same question up to affine equivalence x = Ay + b and identify which types of chaotic attractors can occur, for example Lorenz-type or Rössler-type attractors.

evidence.quote: 1. For a given k and N = 3 after eliminating equivalent systems under the scalar transformations x1 = aX1 , x2 = bX2 , x3 = cX3 , t = δτ ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative?

2. For any given integer N > 3 and k after eliminating equivalent systems under the scalar transformations ... and nth-order permutation groups Pg ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative?

3. More generally for a given N ≥ 3 after eliminating equivalent systems under affine transformations x0 = Ay + b, t = δτ ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative? 4. A related open problem is what types of chaotic attractors can the systems (3.23) have? Two examples of “types” of attractors are Lorenz attractor and Rössler attractor.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider autonomous polynomial ordinary differential systems on R^N of the form

   x_i'(t) = P_i(x_1, ..., x_N),    i = 1, ..., N,

where each P_i is a polynomial of total degree at most k. Call such a system "chaotic" if it admits a bounded invariant set on which the flow exhibits sensitive dependence on initial conditions and a dense orbit (i.e., a chaotic attractor or chaotic invariant set in the standard dynamical-systems sense). Call the system "conservative" if its flow preserves volume (equivalently, div(P) ≡ 0) and "dissipative" if the time-average of div(P) on the attractor is strictly negative.

Two systems are considered equivalent under the following natural group actions:

(a) For N = 3: the diagonal scaling group acting by x_1 = a X_1, x_2 = b X_2, x_3 = c X_3, t = δ τ (with a,b,c,δ nonzero reals), together with the cyclic/symmetric permutation group S_3 acting on coordinates.

(b) For N > 3: the diagonal scaling group acting by x_i = a_i X_i, t = δ τ together with the full symmetric group S_N permuting coordinates.

(c) In general (N ≥ 3): the affine group acting by x = A y + b with A ∈ GL_N(R), b ∈ R^N, combined with time rescaling t = δ τ.

Solve the following:

1. For N = 3 and each fixed k, classify all equivalence classes (under (a)) of polynomial systems of degree at most k that admit chaotic solutions; in particular, determine the exact (finite or otherwise) number of such chaotic equivalence classes, and within them count how many are conservative and how many are dissipative.

2. For each N > 3 and each fixed k, give the analogous classification and counts under the equivalence (b).

3. For each N ≥ 3 and each fixed k, give the analogous classification and counts under the affine equivalence (c).

4. Determine which topological/dynamical types of chaotic attractors (for example Lorenz-type or Rössler-type) can arise among the systems above for each N and k.
artifact.status_search_result: The classification and counting of chaotic polynomial ODE systems up to scaling, permutation, or affine equivalence is a long-standing open program. While extensive empirical/computer-aided searches (e.g., Sprott's lists of simple chaotic flows) have produced many examples and partial enumerations for small N and k, no complete classification or exact counts (including conservative vs. dissipative breakdown) are known for general N and k, nor is the complete list of attainable attractor types. The problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: Some Simple Chaotic Flows (Sprott)
status_evidence.snippet: Empirical lists of simple chaotic polynomial ODE systems are constructed by computer search, but no complete classification up to natural equivalences is provided.
status_evidence.claim: Only partial empirical enumerations exist; no full classification.

status_evidence.title: Elegant Chaos: Algebraically Simple Chaotic Flows (Sprott, 2010)
status_evidence.snippet: Catalogues many chaotic polynomial systems but does not solve the general counting/classification problem up to scaling, permutation, or affine equivalence for arbitrary N and k.
status_evidence.claim: Comprehensive catalogues remain incomplete; general counting is unresolved.
